div.head: Quaestio 2
An inferiores superioribus parere obligentur
div.p: In the last chapter of this distinction, the master speaks about the power of superiors, and on account of this, it is asked whether inferiors are obligated to obey their superiors? This question asks one thing and supposes another. For it asks about the sin of inferiors if they do not obey their superiors, and it supposes that there is some superior power. Thus, in order to provide a clarification of each part I offer conclusions, the first of which will be that, according to reason, there are superiors and inferiors. The second conclusion is that when inferiors disobey the commands of their superiors they commit sin. The third, following directly from this and responding directly to the title of the question, is how the inferior are obliged to obey their superiors.

The first conclusion is proved: something is rationally instituted without which human society is not able to be ruled. But society cannot be maintained without superiority and inferiority. The consequence is clear with the major premise, and the minor premise is proved since, supposing the opposite, evil people would oppress the weak and the good, they would languish in idleness and vice since no one would be there to restrain insolence.
Moreover, during this life, the good would not be rewarded for their good acts and thus few people would be motivated to do good things. Therefore it in conformity with right reason to have superiors in order reward diligent acts and restrain the vicious.
Further among the angels and heavenly citizens there is order and a reduction to a single superior, and since this is so in the triumphant church, so it will be the same in the militant church.
Further, those running the military well have superiority and inferiority, there is one ruler of the military, like Joab in the house of David or Abner in the house of Saul, after them are the centurions, and the deacons which the inferiors have to obey. If this way had not been followed by the Romans and Alexander the Macedon they would not have achieved in military affairs so much glory among those who came after them.
Further, this is clear in the colleges in which a primary person presides under which there are centurions and deacons according to the magnitude of the readings, such that in the convents, you will have an abbot as the prior and in chapters you will have a deacon and archdeacon.
This is clear from the heavens in ordered relation to the elements and the superior elements in ordered relation to the inferior elements. And in the first book of the Meteorology, it is necessary that this inferior world to be touching the superior latitudes, such that its entire virtue (power) is governed in this way, and the inferior spheres are moved by the motion of the first.

The second conclusion is proved whether there temporal or spiritual superiors. In spiritual matters it is clear. Otherwise breaking the fast of Saith Peter or Andrew would not be a sin because it is not part of the divine law. Indeed if you say whoever hears you hears me, whoever spurns you spurns me Luke 10. And thus this transgression is against the divine law.
Against this, in this life every purely human law contrary to all those rightly speaking, and it is necessary that you share this same opinion.
In temporal matters it is clear from Romans 13
Whoever resists authority resists the order of God, and those who resist will bring damnation upon themselves. For rulers do not an obstacle to good works but to evil works . And few words later it connects to what has been proposed about sin.
Therefore it is necessary that you be submissive not only to avoid anger but also on account of conscience. For because of this you pay taxes, for they are minister of God, serving for this very purpose. . For this is the case, those not paying their taxes legitimately imposed commit sin. This is clear from the conclusion and from the words of the apostle saying explicitly:
taxes to whom are owed taxes, revenue to whom are owed revenue, honor to those who are owed honor, and fear to those who are owed fear. . Revenue is a stipend which is given to lords when goods are transported through the country. Tribute is that which is given back for the whole country.
The third conclusion is the corollary following the preceding.

Against the first conclusion it is argued thus: in the state of innocence there would have been no superiority, and at that time equality among every one would have been the law of nature. Therefore, today, superiority is against the law of nature. The consequence holds because the law of nature is invariable since it is a either practical principle evident from the terms or a conclusion deduced from it.

To the first I clarify that statement that no one would have been superior as either according to the utility of the superior as it became useful in the state of fallen nature, and in this way it is conceded, or with respect to the direction to the good for the utility of those directed, and this way I deny it.
No everyone in this state would have been equally wise, prudent, or good, and consequently the less prudent were looking to the more prudent for direction toward the good.
Some at that time would have been born as children and over time would have acquired reasons, just like our own children.
And among the adults some would have had bodies better disposed, in complexion, like Achitofel, but none of these people would have used these natural gifts poorly while in that state. And concerning children, the parents would have taken sufficient that they would not fall in fire or water.
Further with respect assumed proposition, it is said that one proposition at one time is according to the law of nature and in another time its opposite, just as it is in conformity with right reason that a healthy person take wine and food in good quantity, but if they fall into sickness the opposite is in accordance with right reason.

In the second place it is argued against the same conclusion in Hosea 8 I have them a king in my anger, therefore it is not in conformity with right reason to have this superiority. It is responded that some justly rule who from the beginning have a just principle, and some become rulers through tyranny. The second kind are permitted by God as a punishment of the wicked and training for the good, about which it is said in Hosea 8, they reigned but not from me And proverbs 8, through me rulers rule and through me tyrants hold the land.
And when these according to their foolish opinion have attained the height of honor they are frequently thrown by God in the abyss. not only in a future age, but also in this world. This was made clear from the kings of Israel one of whom destroyed the entire house of another on account of the sins of the king and the apostles. And frequently the kings of Assyria, Syria and Egypt were introduced for their extermination so that they would learn to obey the Lord, as it is says in Job 34 He makes a hypocrite to reign on account of the sins of the people. But all just power is from God, just as the apostle says in Romans 13 Every soul is subject to a higher power. For there is no power unless it is from God; and those that exist are ordained by God. And this also proves the conclusion when Christ said to Pilate: You would have no power over me if it had not been given to you from above.

To the first of these, the antecedent is conceded, and also the negative consequence, that if it is against the law of God, it is not a law by the reason of the law, namely, that it is pleasing that it be conformed to the divine law, that is, that it not be turned against it, or we speak of law properly spoken.

When kings impose more taxes than is fair, they act wrongly. It is not the duty of a king, but rather a royal function that is undermined when the king does not look out for the common good, but instead collects for his own particular good, neglecting the common good. At that point, according to Aristotle, he is called a tyrant. In a particular case, it is difficult to render a verdict without knowing the reason. In general, it is true that the people are bound to provide the king with the necessary things for his status and the utility of the republic. However, in all things, it is safer to doubt when it comes to paying a debt, and even if there is no immediate need, it may become necessary in a few years. It is more difficult to impose new taxes than to continue those already imposed. But if, according to the judgment of prudent men, there is sufficient reason for the present and impending danger, the king is bound to cut back on part of it, lest the people be burdened, for if the cause is removed, the effect ceases. Darius, the father of Xerxes, is greatly praised because when a war was impending and money was needed, he summoned the governors and princes of the provinces and asked them not to impose taxes, and when they replied that they had only collected a moderate amount, he ordered them to give half of it back to the people. For he valued the goodwill of the people more than the amount of money, and if this pagan noble did so, Christian princes ought to do so all the more. Therefore, sometimes the collection of money for the construction of bridges or for repelling an enemy of the kingdom is poorly continued, even though its origin was reasonable. It is now clear that powerful and long-lasting constructions have been built, and sometimes there is no apparent war to be fought. Or, if it happens, it is enough to resist the enemy with the money already in the treasury. Indeed, if more money is collected from the people because of a great and imminent war, and if peace is made without the need for money, which, according to the judgment of prudent men, will bring stability, the money is owed to the people who contributed it. It is inhumane to squander the money of the poor people, considering the labors and hardships they endure. If this is done as it should be, the people will willingly accept even harsher taxes in the future, judging from past experiences that the king will use the money for the utility of the republic. But if the money is not returned, I speak of places where it is customary to impose taxes in this way, where the people go to war at their own expense to defend their country or to invade the enemy, it is not right to impose expenses on the people when they are already providing equally by going to war at their own expense.

It is doubted what if a father calls his son to some duty, and at the same time the king calls him to war, to whom he is bound to obey. The same is clear regarding a religious person, whether he is bound to obey the abbot or the Roman pontiff when they give opposing commands at the same time.
Secondly, it is doubted regarding the prelature of the religious whether, if the abbot orders a religious person to reveal a hidden sin of a brother, he will be bound to obey.

o the first doubt, it is responded that either the king commands irrationally and the father rationally, and then one should obey the father unless he fears death would be inflicted on him if he doesn't go to war when summoned. If both request rationally, such that the father wants to cultivate the fields and the king orders going to war, then for the common good, the king should be obeyed and the father neglected. And I understand the father's rational command absolutely if the king's command did not intervene, because there is a general rule in this matter: when those having superior and inferior jurisdictions command incompatible things, one should obey the superior, and this is so if they command in those things in which the superiority and inferiority extend; but if one is not superior with regard to such an office, no consideration should be given to him, as if an archbishop commanded something and an exempt abbot commanded something else, one should obey the abbot. This rule is from St. Augustine's book "On the Nature of Good" and the Master cites the letter which says: "If a power commands something you ought not do, then despise that power, fearing the greater power; consider the degrees of human affairs. If a procurator commands something, should it be done if he commands against the proconsul? Again, if the proconsul commands something and the emperor commands something else, is it doubted that, having despised the former, one should serve the latter?" Therefore, if the emperor commands one thing and God commands another, having despised the former, one should obey God. From this, it is clear that if the Roman Pontiff commands a monk to go to preach in Livonia or among the Ruthenians, who can well exercise that province, and the abbot commands the opposite, one is bound to obey the Pontiff. It is clear, although both commands are rational in part, that one should obey the superior according to Augustine's rule in that which he is superior, as in the proposed case, and similarly, it should be said if an abbot and a prior or a prior and a subprior command opposite things.

To the second doubt, the response is given: or one proceeds by the way of denunciation, that is, to the castigation of the negligent religious, in no way is he bound to reveal the hidden fault of a brother to the abbot, but according to the evangelical rule, "If your brother sins against you," one is not to obey the abbot against the precept of God. Rather, the reputation of the brother is to be preserved from the sin that hinders, and lest it become sullied in the eyes of his superior. In an inquiry, infamy ought to precede, and in accusation similarly, where the intention is to punish the sinner for the good of the multitude. If infamy precedes, the prelate can investigate the truth, and his subjects are bound to obey him, because the prelate proceeds in his spiritual forum just as a lay judge in his own, and this can be proven through many chapters: extra de purga, canon "patet," chapter "moniales," and chapter "quotiens," where it is stated that when someone is defamed against whom a crime cannot be proven, he ought to clear himself with an oath of truth.
